## claude.ai Crypto.com
Crypto.com Exchange MCP Server - Real-time cryptocurrency market data and interactive widgets.

Available Tools:
- get_widget: Get any interactive widget by name (orderbook, trades, candles)
- get_market_orderbook: Order book snapshot (bids/asks)

- _OUTLOOK: Draft a fully-formatted email into Outlook for Mac — opens a ready-to-review compose window, never sends. Drives classic Outlook via AppleScript with HTML content so paragraphs, bullet lists, and numbered lists render correctly; degrades to a plain-text mailto draft if only New Outlook is present. Pulls recipient addresses from CONTACTS.md and writes in Nick's email voice. USE WHEN draft an email, write an email to X, email X about Y, open a draft in Outlook, compose an email, reply to X, send an email (draft it for review). NOT FOR actually transmitting mail unattended (this is draft-only), Gmail/web mail (no Outlook desktop), or bulk/broadcast sends (use _BROADCAST). Mac only — requires osascript.
- Agents: Compose CUSTOM agents from Base Traits + Voice + Specialization, and manage predefined functional TEAMS. Traits combine expertise (security, technical, research), personality (skeptical, analytical, enthusiastic), and approach (thorough, rapid, systematic). ComposeAgent.ts merges base + user config, outputs unique prompt + ElevenLabs voice + prosody. Predefined teams: engineering, architecture, marketing, design, security, research, content, strategy — each YAML-configured with roles, tensions, and specialist members. Observer team variant: read-only oversight agents that vote continue/halt/escalate against the tool-activity audit log (high-blast-radius or unattended runs only). USE WHEN create custom agents, spin up agents, specialized agents, agent personalities, available traits, list traits, agent voices, compose agent, spawn parallel agents, launch agents, engineering team, architecture team, marketing team, design team, security team, research team, content team, strategy team, get the team on this, observer team, audit agents. NOT FOR ad-hoc swarms or TeamCreate coordination (use Delegation). NOT FOR single-threaded delegation without unique identities (use Delegation Task).
- ApertureOscillation: 3-pass scope oscillation that holds a question constant while shifting the scope envelope — narrow/tactical, wide/strategic, then synthesis — to surface design tensions invisible at any single zoom level. Requires two distinct inputs: the tactical target (what you're building) and strategic context (the larger system it serves). Pass 1 captures the component's own internal logic. Pass 2 reveals what the system needs it to be. Pass 3 finds where those views diverge — that delta is the output. Produces: design tensions, scope recommendations, and coherence assessments. Single workflow: Workflows/Oscillate.md. BPE-fragile — quarterly test recommended to verify smarter models don't naturally oscillate scope without prompting. Best integration point: Algorithm OBSERVE phase (before ISC) or THINK phase (before approach commitment). NOT a lens rotation (that's IterativeDepth) and NOT idea generation (that's BeCreative). NOT FOR deep incident causal chains (use RootCauseAnalysis) or assumption decomposition (use FirstPrinciples). USE WHEN aperture oscillation, oscillate scope, zoom in and out, tactical vs strategic, scope framing, design tension, architecture decision, feature fits system, system coherence check, local vs global design, build this inside that, wrong scope, design review, scope negotiation.
- Aphorisms: Manages a curated aphorism collection with full CRUD — content-based matching, themed search, thinker research, and database maintenance. Organizes quotes by author, theme, context, and newsletter usage history to prevent repetition. Four workflows: FindAphorism (analyze newsletter content, match themes, return 3-5 ranked recommendations with rationale), AddAphorism (parse quote + author, extract themes, validate uniqueness, update theme index), ResearchThinker (deep research on philosopher, add sourced quotes to database), SearchAphorisms (search by theme, keyword, or author). Database at ~/.claude/skills/aphorisms/Database/aphorisms.md — stores full quote text, author attribution, theme tags, context/background, source reference, and usage history per entry. Theme index supports 12+ categories: Work Ethic, Resilience, Learning, Stoicism, Risk, Wisdom, Truth-seeking, Excellence, Curiosity, Freedom, Rationality, Clarity. Supported thinkers: Hitchens, Feynman, Deutsch, Sam Harris, Spinoza, plus any requested author. Newsletter integration: tracks which quotes used in which issues to enforce variety; content theme extraction drives automated matching. USE WHEN: aphorism, quote, saying, find a quote, research thinker, add aphorism, search aphorisms, quote for newsletter, what did X say about, quotes about [topic], quote bank, find matching quote, quote collection, add this quote, check usage history. NOT FOR general creative writing or social media post generation — those go through dedicated writing/social skill…
- Apify: Scrape social media platforms, business data, and e-commerce via Apify actors — Instagram profiles/posts/hashtags/comments, LinkedIn profiles/jobs/posts, TikTok profiles/hashtags/videos/comments, YouTube channels/search/comments, Facebook posts/groups/comments, Google Maps business search with contact/review/image extraction, Amazon products/reviews/pricing, and general-purpose multi-page web crawling with custom pageFunction extraction logic. File-based TypeScript wrappers (scrapeInstagramProfile, searchGoogleMaps, scrapeAmazonProduct, scrapeWebsite, etc.) filter and transform data in code before returning to model context, achieving 95-99% token savings over direct MCP protocol. Parallel multi-platform queries via Promise.all for social listening dashboards. Lead enrichment pipeline: Google Maps → qualified filter → optional LinkedIn enrichment. Competitive analysis across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok simultaneously. USE WHEN scrape Instagram, scrape LinkedIn, scrape TikTok, scrape YouTube, scrape Facebook, Google Maps leads, Amazon reviews, business intelligence, multi-platform social listening, competitive analysis, lead generation, social monitoring, Apify actors, web crawl, extract contacts. NOT FOR X/Twitter bookmarks (use a dedicated X-API skill) or progressive scraping (use BrightData).
- Art: Generates static visual content across 20+ formats via Flux, Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro), and GPT-Image-1. Covers blog header illustrations, editorial art, Mermaid flowcharts, technical architecture diagrams, D3.js dashboards, taxonomies, timelines, 2x2 framework matrices, comparisons, annotated screenshots, recipe cards, aphorism/quote cards, conceptual maps, stat cards, comic panels, YouTube thumbnails, PAI pack icons, and brand-logo wallpapers. Named workflows: Essay, D3Dashboards, Visualize, Mermaid, TechnicalDiagrams, Taxonomies, Timelines, Frameworks, Comparisons, AnnotatedScreenshots, RecipeCards, Aphorisms, Maps, Stats, Comics, YouTubeThumbnailChecklist, AdHocYouTubeThumbnail, CreatePAIPackIcon, LogoWallpaper, RemoveBackground. SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS loads PREFERENCES.md, CharacterSpecs.md, and SceneConstruction.md. --remove-bg flag produces transparent-background PNG (can produce black backgrounds — verify visually). Up to 14 reference images per request (5 human, 6 object Gemini API limit). Output staged to ~/Downloads/ for preview before any project directory copy. Nano Banana Pro uses --size for resolution tier 1K/2K/4K and separate --aspect-ratio. USE WHEN: art, illustration, diagram, flowchart, infographic, header image, thumbnail, visualize, generate image, mermaid, architecture diagram, comic, icon, blog art, framework diagram, D3 chart, remove background, wallpaper. NOT FOR video or animation (use Remotion). NOT FOR the user's personal portrait/headshot (use a dedicated headshot skill).
- ArXiv: Search and retrieve arXiv academic papers by topic, category, or paper ID — with AlphaXiv-enriched AI-generated overviews. Uses arXiv Atom API (no auth) for discovery and search across cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL (NLP/LLMs), cs.CR (security), cs.MA (multi-agent), cs.SE, and cs.IR. Supports title (ti:), abstract (abs:), author (au:), and category (cat:) search fields with boolean operators (AND, OR, ANDNOT); sorts by lastUpdatedDate or relevance; paginates up to 2,000 results per call with 3s rate limit between calls. AlphaXiv enrichment fetches markdown summaries from alphaxiv.org/overview/{ID}.md; full text from alphaxiv.org/abs/{ID}.md as fallback; 404 means summary not yet generated. Workflows: Latest (new papers by category), Search (topic/keyword search), Paper (single paper deep-dive by ID or URL). API returns Atom XML — parse with text processing, not jq. HTTPS required with -L flag; check published date not lastUpdatedDate for truly new submissions. Output: paper title, authors, abstract, AlphaXiv summary, and direct arXiv URL. USE WHEN arxiv, papers, latest papers, research papers, new papers, what's new in AI research, recent ML papers, paper lookup, arxiv search, find paper by ID, summarize paper, latest NLP research, latest LLM papers, multi-agent papers, cs.AI latest, AI safety papers, software engineering papers, information retrieval papers. NOT FOR general web research (use Research), extracting content from arbitrary URLs (use Parser), or cybersecurity annual report analysis (use AnnualReports).
- AudioEditor: AI-powered audio and video editing pipeline: Whisper word-level transcription (insanely-fast-whisper on MPS) → Claude segment classification (KEEP / CUT_FILLER / CUT_FALSE_START / CUT_STUTTER / CUT_DEAD_AIR / CUT_EDIT_MARKER) → ffmpeg execution with 40ms qsin crossfades and room-tone gap fill → optional Cleanvoice API cloud polish for mouth sounds and loudness normalization. Distinguishes rhetorical pauses from accidental ones. Breaths attenuated to 50% volume (not removed). Preview mode (--preview flag) shows proposed cuts without modifying audio. Aggressive mode (--aggressive flag) applies tighter filler detection thresholds. Polish step (--polish flag) uploads to Cleanvoice API for mouth sound removal and loudness normalization — confirm before cloud upload of sensitive content. Pipeline tools: Transcribe.ts, Analyze.ts, Edit.ts, Polish.ts, Pipeline.ts. Single workflow: Clean.md. Requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; CLEANVOICE_API_KEY optional for polish step. USE WHEN: clean audio, edit audio, remove filler words, clean podcast, remove ums, cut dead air, polish audio, trim recording, audio cleanup, cut stutters, edit interview recording, preview edits, aggressive clean. NOT FOR video composition or animation (use Remotion).
- BeCreative: Divergent ideation and corpus expansion using Verbalized Sampling + extended thinking. Single-shot mode generates 5 internally diverse candidates (p<0.10 each) and surfaces the strongest. # PD Decode and Fit Map - Virgin Senior AI Engineer

How to use this doc: this turns the position description into a fit map so you know, before you walk in, where you are obviously strong, where you bridge from adjacent experience, and where the honest gaps are and how to handle them. Round 1 is run by Harry (engineer who started when Jaimyn did) and the engineering lead. Round 2, if you get there, is the Head of AI and possibly Jaimyn.

---

## The role in one line
Senior AI Engineer, CIO Division / AI team, Brisbane, reports to Head of AI, Level 2B, no direct reports. A hands-on applied-AI plus full-stack engineer who ships production AI systems and is trusted with the delivery realities: testing, evaluation, observability, safe rollout, and stakeholder communication. # AI Safety Systems - Virgin Senior AI Engineer

How to use this doc: Jaimyn named safety as a co-equal pillar with RAG and evals, so it gets its own treatment here rather than living as one section of the AI fundamentals doc. Read it out loud. This is genuinely your home ground, you put guardrails around generative AI in a regulated bank, which is one of the few settings stricter than a customer-facing airline. The aim is to talk about AI safety as an engineering discipline with layers, failure modes, and controls, not as a vague "we make it safe" gesture.

Your strongest framing for this whole topic: AI safety is the same discipline as any safety-critical or compliance control. You identify the failure modes, you control for them in proportion to their blast radius, and you make it auditable. You have done exactly that in banking, and in literal coastal emergency operations through LIMSOC.

---

## 1. What "AI safety systems" means in production
Be precise, because the phrase is overloaded. There are two levels:
- **Model-level safety (alignment):** what the model provider (OpenAI, Anthropic) does to make the base model refuse harmful requests, reduce bias, and behave. You mostly inherit this, you do not build it.
- **System-level safety (your job):** the controls you build around the model to keep your application inside acceptable behaviour. This is what an AI engineer owns: guardrails on what goes in, what comes out, and what the system is allowed to do.

When they ask about safety, answer at the system level, that is the engineering. The one-line definition to have ready: "AI safety systems are the controls that keep an AI application inside acceptable behaviour across three surfaces, the input, the output, and any actions it can take, because the model itself is probabilistic and can be manipulated."

## 2. The failure modes (know the threat surface)
You cannot design controls without naming what you are controlling for. The main ones:
- **Hallucination:** confident, plausible, wrong output. A safety issue the moment a customer acts on it (a wrong fare, a wrong baggage rule).
- **Prompt injection:** untrusted text hijacks the model's instructions. The signature LLM-specific attack (see section 4).
- **Jailbreaks:** users coaxing the model past its guardrails to produce disallowed output.

# AI Systems Fundamentals - Virgin Senior AI Engineer

How to use this doc: this is the core of what Jaimyn told you to brush up on (RAG, safety, evals) plus the agentic and LLMOps material the PD leans on. Read it out loud. The goal is not to memorise definitions, it is to be able to explain each idea in your own words and then connect it to something you have actually built. Your ANZ Plus generative-AI search work is a real RAG system, so most of this you have lived, you just need the vocabulary tight.

Your single strongest move in this interview: when they ask about RAG, evals, or guardrails in the abstract, answer the concept cleanly in two sentences, then say "the way this showed up for me was..." and ground it in the ANZ Plus AI search platform. That converts a knowledge question into a credibility moment.

---

## 1. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)

### Mental model
RAG is giving a language model the right context at query time instead of relying on what is baked into its weights. You retrieve relevant documents from an external store, put them in the prompt, and ask the model to answer grounded in that material. It exists because models have a training cut-off, do not know your private data, and hallucinate when they answer from nothing.

### The pipeline (be able to draw this)
1. **Ingestion / indexing (offline):** take source documents, split them into chunks, run each chunk through an embedding model to get a vector, store the vector plus the original text and metadata in a vector store.
2. **Retrieval (at query time):** embed the user's query with the same model, do a similarity search (nearest neighbours) against the store, get the top-k chunks.
3. **Augmentation:** pack those chunks into the prompt as context, usually with the instruction "answer only from the provided context, and say you do not know if it is not there".
4. **Generation:** the model produces the answer grounded in the retrieved context, ideally with citations back to the source chunks.

### Senior nuance (this is where depth shows)

# FastAPI and FastMCP Fundamentals: Interview Brushup

This is a confidence-and-articulation doc, not a reference manual: read each topic's mental model and the "speakable" answers out loud until you can say them in your own words without notes. You know REST, gRPC, HTTP, DI, and async deeply already, so most of this is mapping concepts you own onto Python names, not learning new ideas.

## How FastAPI and FastMCP connect to the Virgin role

Virgin's CIO/AI team runs a live flight-search experience inside ChatGPT, built on OpenAI's ChatGPT Apps platform. ChatGPT Apps are MCP-based: the app is a remote MCP server that exposes tools (like flight search) which the model calls on the user's behalf. FastMCP is the Pythonic framework for building those MCP servers, and it is deliberately shaped like FastAPI. So the stack is almost certainly: FastAPI for normal HTTP/AI service endpoints, FastMCP for the tools ChatGPT calls, both async, both Pydantic-typed. If you can talk about FastAPI's async model and Pydantic, FastMCP follows naturally, because it reuses the same mental furniture.

The one-sentence version to have ready: "FastAPI is the async Python web framework for building the AI service APIs, and FastMCP is the same idea applied to MCP, so the flight-search tools Virgin exposes to ChatGPT are almost certainly FastMCP tools."

---

# PART 1: FastAPI

## ASGI vs WSGI, and why async matters

**Mental model.** WSGI is the old synchronous Python web standard: one worker handles one request at a time, blocking until it finishes. ASGI is the async successor: a single worker can hold thousands of in-flight requests, suspending each one while it waits on I/O and doing other work in the meantime. FastAPI is built on ASGI, which is what lets it handle high-concurrency I/O-bound workloads (calling an LLM, hitting a database, fanning out to other services) on a small number of workers.

**Senior nuance.** Async only helps when you are I/O-bound, not CPU-bound. The whole point is the event loop reclaims the thread while you wait on the network. If you do heavy CPU work inside an async handler, you block the event loop and stall every other concurrent request on that worker. For AI workloads this matters enormously: an LLM call can take many seconds, and during that wait one async worker can serve hundreds of other requests instead of sitting idle.


=== 04a-javascript-and-typescript.md (365 lines) ===
# JavaScript and TypeScript Language Fundamentals: Interview Brushup

How to use this doc: each topic gives you a mental model, the senior nuance worth signalling, likely pointed questions with speakable answers in your voice, and a bridge from Go/Java or your real frontend work. Read the answers aloud once; the goal is confident verbal articulation in a conversational round, not memorised perfection.

---

## 1. Single-threaded model and the event loop

**Mental model.** JavaScript runs your code on a single thread with a single call stack, so only one thing executes at a time. It stays responsive by being non-blocking: anything async (timers, network, file IO) is handed off, and when it finishes its callback is queued to run later. The event loop is the thing that pulls work off those queues onto the stack when the stack is empty.

**The senior nuance.** There are two queues, not one, and they have different priority. The microtask queue (resolved promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`) is fully drained after every single task before the event loop touches the macrotask queue (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, IO callbacks, UI events). So a resolved promise always runs before a `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, even though the timeout looks like it should fire immediately. That ordering is the classic depth probe.

**If they ask...**

- *"What is the event loop?"* "JavaScript is single-threaded, one call stack. When the stack is empty, the event loop checks the queues for callbacks that are ready and pushes them onto the stack to run. That loop is how a single thread handles concurrency without blocking."
- *"What logs first: a setTimeout zero or a resolved promise's then?"* "The promise. Both are async, but promise callbacks go on the microtask queue and timeouts go on the macrotask queue. After the current synchronous code finishes, the loop drains all microtasks before it runs a single macrotask, so the `.then` runs before the `setTimeout`, even at zero delay."
- *"Does setTimeout zero run immediately?"* "No. It runs after the current synchronous code and after all pending microtasks. Zero is the minimum delay, not a guarantee. It schedules the callback as a macrotask for the next pass of the loop."
- *"How does it stay responsive if it's single-threaded?"* "The expensive waiting, network and timers and IO, happens off-thread in the browser or runtime. JavaScript just registers a callback and keeps going. The thread only blocks if you write genuinely synchronous heavy work, like a big loop, which is the thing you avoid."

**Bridge.** In Go you reach for goroutines and channels for concurrency; in Java you have threads and an executor pool. JavaScript gives you neither: it is cooperative concurrency on one thread, and you never block it. The mental flip from Go is that you do not spawn workers for IO. You hand IO off and let the event loop call you back. The blocking sin in JS is the equivalent of holding a lock on the only thread you have.

# React Hooks and Modern React: Verbal Brushup for the Virgin AI Round 1

How to use this doc: read each topic out loud, then close the laptop and re-explain the mental model and the "senior nuance" in your own words until it is automatic. The "If they ask" answers are scripts to internalise the shape of a strong reply, not lines to recite, so practise speaking them in your own phrasing.

---

## 0. Framing the whole conversation

You are a senior, back-end-leaning engineer who ships real React. Lead with that posture. You have built a real-time portal at Macquarie, led a Flash-to-modern rewrite at Leidos, and you run a production Next.js App Router SaaS solo. You do not need to bluff depth you do not have. The strong move when you hit your edge is "I know the shape of this and here is how I would reason about it", not silence and not invention.

One sentence to have ready if they ask how you rate yourself on front-end: "I am a competent senior on React, strongest on architecture, data flow, and state, less of a pixel-level CSS specialist, and I have shipped the modern stack including Server Components in AccessBuddy."

---

## 1. useState and why state is immutable

**Mental model.** useState gives a component a piece of memory that survives re-renders, plus a setter. Calling the setter tells React "this value changed, schedule a re-render". The value you read in a render is a snapshot, fixed for that render. You never mutate it in place, you call the setter with a new value and React re-renders with the new snapshot.

**Senior nuance.** Two things signal depth here. First, state updates are asynchronous and batched, so after you call setCount you do not see the new value on the next line, you see it on the next render. Second, when the new state depends on the old state you pass a function, setCount(c => c + 1), not setCount(count + 1). The functional form reads the latest queued value, so three increments in a row actually add three. The literal form closes over a stale snapshot and you lose updates. Immutability matters because React decides whether to re-render by comparing references, so mutating an object or array in place can leave the reference unchanged and the UI stale.

# Senior Python Fundamentals: Virgin AI Engineer Round 1 Brushup

## 1. The data model and dunder methods

**Mental model.** Almost everything in Python is an object, and behaviour is driven by special methods with double underscores, the "dunders". `len(x)` calls `x.__len__()`, `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`, `x[i]` calls `x.__getitem__(i)`. You make your own types behave like built-ins by implementing these. It is structural: the interpreter doesn't care what your class is, only which protocol methods it implements.

**Senior nuance.** The data model is Python's version of operator overloading plus interface conformance rolled together, but driven by convention not declaration. `__repr__` vs `__str__` matters: `__repr__` is for developers and debugging (unambiguous), `__str__` is for users (readable). `__eq__` and `__hash__` must stay consistent, and if you define `__eq__` without `__hash__` your object becomes unhashable, which silently breaks set and dict membership.

## 1. What a ChatGPT App actually is

In October 2025 OpenAI launched the Apps SDK and Apps in ChatGPT, a way for third parties to build applications that run inside the ChatGPT conversation. Users browse an app directory (the "add-in" library Nick mentioned), connect an app, and then invoke it inside chat by typing "+" or just by asking something the app handles. Virgin Australia partnered with OpenAI and shipped flight search this way (announced November 2025, CEO Dave Emerson called it "a significant milestone").

The crucial technical fact: **ChatGPT Apps are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP)**. A developer builds and hosts an MCP server that exposes tools (and optionally resources and prompts), ChatGPT acts as the MCP client, and OpenAI's Apps SDK adds a UI layer on top so the app can render rich interactive components inline in the chat, not just text.

So an app has three parts:
1. **An MCP server** you build and host, exposing tools the model can call (for Virgin: search flights, find reward seats, get fares).
2. **A UI layer** via the Apps SDK, optional, that lets the app return custom rendered components (a flight-results card, a date-price grid) inside the conversation rather than plain text.
3. **A connection/auth layer**, OAuth, so the app can act on behalf of a logged-in user and reach their account data (Velocity points balance, bookings).

# PD Decode and Fit Map - Virgin Senior AI Engineer

How to use this doc: this turns the position description into a fit map so you know, before you walk in, where you are obviously strong, where you bridge from adjacent experience, and where the honest gaps are and how to handle them. Round 1 is run by Harry (engineer who started when Jaimyn did) and the engineering lead. Round 2, if you get there, is the Head of AI and possibly Jaimyn.

---

## The role in one line
Senior AI Engineer, CIO Division / AI team, Brisbane, reports to Head of AI, Level 2B, no direct reports. A hands-on applied-AI plus full-stack engineer who ships production AI systems and is trusted with the delivery realities: testing, evaluation, observability, safe rollout, and stakeholder communication. This is an individual-contributor senior role with mentoring expectations, not a management role.

## What Virgin actually wants (read between the lines)
The PD says it three times in different words: "recognising the realities of delivery, trade-offs and compromise", "what it takes to deliver production-ready solutions, including testing, evaluation and observability", "technical excellence while recognising the realities of delivery". They have been burned by, or are guarding against, people who can prototype with an LLM but cannot operate it in production. Your entire career is production engineering rigour in regulated, high-stakes environments. That is the centre of your fit. Lead with it.

---

Straight answer up front: two of these three concerns are smaller than you think, and the third one I'd handle very differently from how you're proposing. Let me take them in order, then push back on the LIMSOC plan because I think it's the riskiest move in the interview, not the safest.

## 1. Full-stack — you're underrating yourself

You have more full-stack proof than you're crediting. AccessBuddy is a live, multi-tenant SaaS you built solo end to end: Next.js frontend, Hono/Bun API, Postgres, GCP, plus the operational layer (observability, CI/CD, auth, payments). That is *more* end-to-end ownership than most engineers who call themselves full-stack, because you own the ops too. Add the Macquarie real-time portal (React/TypeScript) and the Leidos rewrite and you have front-end, back-end, and infra across three independent contexts.

The prep pack tells you to keep AccessBuddy supplementary — that guidance is right *for the AI-depth narrative*. But if a full-stack question lands, AccessBuddy is the answer, and you lead with it without apology. Your concern here isn't a real gap, it's a framing habit. Reframe: "full-stack isn't something I dabble in, I've shipped and operated a production SaaS solo."

## 2. Go depth — largely irrelevant for this role

Virgin's PD is **Python-primary**. Go is not a requirement. So depth-of-Go is a gap against a bar that doesn't exist here. Do not volunteer Go as a strength and then get probed on runtime internals — that's how you create a hole. Position it as: polyglot systems engineer, deepest in Go and Java, fluent in Python, reasons about all of them from a systems base. If someone asks directly how deep your Go is, "I've used it as a supporting language, my deepest production work is Java and Go-adjacent systems" is a clean, senior answer. This one you can basically stop worrying about.

## 3. AI breadth — real concern, but the LIMSOC plan is the wrong fix

Here's where I'll push back hard, and it's tactical, not moral.

**Don't claim you built and shipped POCs you designed on paper.** Three reasons, in order of how much they'll hurt you:

- **The Head of AI is exactly the person who probes implementation.** Round 1 was pointed. Round 2 with the Head of AI is *more* likely to go "which embedding model, what was your chunking strategy, how did you eval it, what was p95 latency, what broke." A real POC has scar tissue and specific numbers. A paper design doesn't. The moment you can't produce the texture of something you claim you built, a senior interviewer smells it — not because they can verify externally, but because *builders sound different from designers* and they know the difference cold. That's the trap: "they can't verify I didn't" is true for the org, but not for the person across the table who has built these things.

- **You don't need to bluff, because the honest version is genuinely strong.** "I designed seven applied-AI initiatives for LIMSOC — entity extraction, RAG-backed SOP coaching, ETA prediction — and scoped how I'd build, eval, and operate each" is a *staff-level* statement. Architecture and design judgment is what distinguishes senior from mid. Initiative 6 (ETA prediction, where you argue *not* to use an LLM) is a better credibility signal than a fake shipped POC, because knowing when not to reach for an LLM is exactly the production maturity Virgin's PD keeps hammering.

- **One deep system + fluent reasoning is a legitimate senior profile.** Nobody senior has shipped every AI pattern. Your move is depth on ANZ Plus (you owned real retrieval/search on Vertex + Gemini in a compliance-critical context — that's rare and real), then reason credibly about the rest from that base. Breadth faked reads as junior; depth owned plus honest bridges reads as senior. Your own prep pack already says this on line 82 of the fit doc, and it's right.

So the reframe for AI breadth: **stop trying to look broad. Look deep on one thing and disciplined about the rest.** Lead with ANZ (built, operated, real numbers), follow with LIMSOC as *design/architecture* work honestly labelled, and treat "I haven't shipped X but here's how I'd approach it" as a strength, not a confession.

## The one line that ties it together
Your genuine edge over other candidates is the ANZ production-AI-in-a-regulated-bank experience plus solo SaaS operational ownership. That combination is uncommon and it's all true. The fastest way to *lose* that edge is to bolt a fabrication onto it that a sharp Head of AI unravels in two follow-up questions, because then everything true you said gets re-examined too. Honesty here isn't the ethical choice, it's the winning one.

If it's helpful, I can draft the exact LIMSOC framing lines — the honest "designed and scoped" version with the depth cues that make design work sound as senior as it actually is — so you're not improvising the boundary live.

Got it — that changes point 2 materially, because Python *is* the primary language for this role. So this is a real gap, not an irrelevant one. Here's the revised advice on it (points 1 and 3 stand as I gave them).

## 2. In-depth Python — real gap, but you close it two ways, and one of them is action this week

**Recommendation: don't try to sound like a Python native. Do two things instead — bridge from systems depth, and actually write some Python before round 2 so you're not speaking purely theoretically.**

### Why the gap is manageable
A Python-primary senior role does not hire on language trivia — it hires on judgment, systems thinking, and whether you'll ship safely. You have that in surplus. The concepts that make Python Python — the GIL and why threading isn't parallelism, async/await, generators, context managers, decorators, typing/Pydantic — are all things you already understand *as concepts* from Go and Java (goroutines vs asyncio, channels, defer≈context managers, interfaces≈protocols/duck typing). A senior polyglot who reasons about Python from first principles reads *better* than a mid-level engineer who memorised idioms but can't explain the runtime. Your `05-senior-python.md` doc is built exactly on these Go/Java bridges — that's the right spine.

### Where you can actually get caught
The pointed-question risk isn't "do you know Python," it's a specific probe where a systems person bluffs and trips. The ones to be genuinely solid on, out loud:
- **GIL** — what it is, why CPU-bound threading doesn't scale, and the real answer (multiprocessing / async for I/O-bound / releasing the GIL in C extensions). This is the single most common senior Python probe.
- **async/await and the event loop** — and crucially *when* async helps (I/O-bound) vs when it doesn't (CPU-bound). This ties straight into FastAPI.
- **Generators / iterators** and why they matter for memory.
- **Decorators and context managers** — what they desugar to.
- **Typing + Pydantic** — because it's how FastAPI does validation, and it's the bridge from your strong typed-language background.

### The highest-leverage move: make the gap partly untrue before round 2
The fastest way to convert this concern is to spend a few hours writing Python. Stand up a tiny FastAPI service with a Pydantic model and an async endpoint, and ideally a minimal FastMCP server. Two payoffs:

1. It makes your FastAPI/FastMCP bridge *real* — you can honestly say "I've been building with FastAPI and FastMCP recently" instead of "I've done the reading," which is a materially stronger and completely true line.
2. It gives your Python answers the texture of recent hands-on work, which is exactly what a Head-of-AI probe is listening for.

This also directly de-risks concern 3 — an MCP server is the thing Virgin's own ChatGPT flight-search app is built on, so a weekend FastMCP build lets you speak to their flagship product from experience, not theory. One afternoon of building hits your Python gap, your FastAPI gap, and your AI-breadth gap simultaneously. That's the play.

### The honest line if asked directly
"Python's not the language I've gone deepest in — that's Java and Go — but I'm fluent in it and I reason about it from a systems base. I've been building with FastAPI and Pydantic recently, and the concepts I care about — concurrency model, the GIL, async, typing — transfer cleanly." Clean, senior, true, and it pivots to what you *have* done rather than parking on the gap.

Net: Python is your most legitimate concern of the three, but it's the one most fixable with a few hours of actual building — and that same building doubles as your best AI-breadth and FastMCP credibility. If you tell me roughly how many days you have before round 2, I'll give you a tight build-and-drill plan that sequences the Python/FastAPI/FastMCP hours against reading `05` and `06` aloud.

# Round 2 - Tom (Head of AI) - Deep Technical Drill + Revision Plan

This is the master doc for round 2. It is built directly on what Jaimyn told you about Tom and the interview style. Read this first, then work the revision plan at the bottom. Interview is **Friday 3 July, 3:30pm**.

---

## The intel (verbatim signal from Jaimyn)
- Tom is the interviewer. He is **extremely experienced and deeply technically skilled.**
- He will **drill down deep wherever he thinks your skills might be weaker, to find your limits.** This is a limit-finding interview by design.
- The style is **bespoke and adaptive** - built on how you answer, digging deeper into your thinking as you go. Socratic, not a fixed script.
- Prepare by **knowing React hooks, JavaScript, and Python fundamentals well.** Expect questions on **memory management, thread management, async/promises, garbage collection.**
- Literal example questions given: **"explain the best you can how the useState hook works"** and **"how does the JavaScript event loop work."**
- **The one deal-breaker:** lack of technical skill, OR **a mismatch between your resume and what you actually did.**
- **The opening move:** the first thing they ask is for you to **pick a good recent project or two on a similar AI tech stack and talk about it really well, focused on productionisation (observability, safety, reliability).** That answer **sets the direction for the rest of the interview.**
- Logistics signal (delivered as a joke about a prior candidate): be on time, dressed properly, in a quiet professional setting. Do not turn up late, in a hoody and cap, walking around a park.

---

## What this interview actually is
Not a strategy conversation. Not "where does AI give Virgin leverage." That was my earlier read and it was wrong. This is a **deep technical depth interview** run by a very strong engineer whose explicit method is to push on each area until he finds the edge of what you actually know.

Two consequences flow from that, and they govern everything:

1. **He will reach your limit. That is the point, and it is fine.** Hitting the edge of your knowledge is expected and is not a fail. **Bluffing past the edge is the fail.** The winning behaviour when you hit your limit: reason out loud from fundamentals, state clearly where your certainty ends, and describe how you would find the answer. "I am not certain beyond this point, here is how I would reason about it and here is how I would confirm it" is a senior, passing answer. A confident wrong answer delivered to cover a gap is the losing one, and Tom is specifically good at spotting it.

2. **Honesty is not just ethics here, it is the literal pass/fail gate.** Jaimyn named exactly one deal-breaker beyond raw skill: **resume-vs-reality mismatch.** That kills the idea of claiming you built LIMSOC POCs you only designed. Tom drills. If you open a claim you cannot go three layers deep on, you walk straight into the one thing that fails candidates. Everything you put on the table must be something you can be drilled on and hold. Designed-and-scoped is true and defensible; built-and-shipped is a trap. Label the boundary yourself before he finds it.

---

## The opening move - the most important five minutes
They open by asking you to pick a recent AI project (or two) and talk about it with a **productionisation** focus. This sets the direction of the whole interview, because they drill into **whatever you open with.** So the choice of project is a strategic decision, not a warm-up.

**Rule: open with the project where your depth is deepest AND fully truthful, because that is the ground you will be fighting on for the next 40 minutes.**

### Primary project: ANZ Plus generative-AI search platform
This is the right opener. It is real, it is AI, it is production, it is regulated (so productionisation was non-negotiable), and you owned a specific, defensible slice of it.

- **Own your actual slice, out loud, early.** You owned the **search/retrieval APIs** inside the platform and drove the team's AI integration strategy and guardrails. Say that precisely. Do not narrate the whole platform as if you built all of it - that is exactly the resume-reality gap Tom hunts. Owning a clear slice deeply beats claiming a broad surface thinly.
- **Lead with productionisation, because that is what they asked for and it is your edge:**
  - **Observability:** OpenTelemetry - metrics, logs, traces across the retrieval path. What you measured (latency, retrieval quality signals, failure rates).
  - **Safety / guardrails:** name a *specific* control you put in and *why*, in a context where a wrong answer has compliance consequences.
  - **Reliability:** fallbacks, latency budgets, what happened when retrieval degraded, how you handled model/version changes.
  - **Evaluation:** how you knew retrieval was good enough to ship, and how you would catch regressions.
- **Build the drill-down ladder now.** Under each of the above, write the next two layers of depth, because Tom *will* ask "how" and then "why" and then "what did you trade off." Prepare: the embedding/retrieval approach, chunking, why Vertex/Gemini, how you evaluated grounding, a specific incident or failure mode and what you changed.

### Optional second project: AccessBuddy
Use as the second only if it strengthens the productionisation story, which it does: **solo-built, live, multi-tenant SaaS with real operational ownership** - observability (Sentry, Better Stack), CI/CD, auth, payments, GCP. It proves end-to-end production discipline you own completely and can be drilled on without limit because you built every line. Keep ANZ as the headline; AccessBuddy is the corroborating full-stack + ops proof.

### The LIMSOC boundary (say this cleanly, never blur it)
If LIMSOC comes up: "I **designed and scoped** a set of applied-AI initiatives for LIMSOC - entity extraction, RAG-backed SOP coaching, ETA prediction - including how I would build, evaluate, and operate each. Those are designs, not shipped systems." Then, if he wants depth, go deep on the *design and the reasoning* (initiative 6, ETA prediction, where you argue **not** to use an LLM, is your best card - it signals production judgment). Design work spoken about with real depth reads as senior. A design dressed up as a shipped POC, then unravelled, hits the deal-breaker.

---

## The fundamentals hit-list - drill each to depth
Jaimyn named the exact territory: **memory management, thread management, async/promises, garbage collection**, across **React hooks, JavaScript, Python.** These are the areas Tom will drill. For each, the target is not recognition, it is being able to explain it out loud, in your own words, and survive two "go deeper" follow-ups. Full treatment is in the existing docs; this is the priority map.

| Area | What to be able to explain cold | Doc |
|---|---|---|
| **JS event loop** | Call stack, task (macrotask) queue vs microtask queue, why promises resolve before setTimeout(0), how async/await schedules continuations as microtasks, why long sync work blocks rendering/input | `04a` |
| **JS closures** | What a closure captures, why it matters for hooks (stale closures), memory implications | `04a` |
| **JS garbage collection** | Mark-and-sweep, reachability, what causes leaks (retained references, forgotten listeners, closures over large scope) | `04a` |
| **Promises / async** | Pending/fulfilled/rejected, microtask timing, async/await as sugar over promises, error propagation | `04a` |
| **React useState** | See scripted answer below - fiber slot, call-order/rules-of-hooks, closure over render, setter schedules re-render, batching, functional updates, immutability + Object.is bail-out | `04` |
| **React useEffect / deps** | When effects run, dependency array semantics, cleanup, why the deps lint rule exists (stale closures again) | `04` |
| **Python memory management** | Reference counting as primary mechanism, generational GC for cycles, when objects are freed | `05` |
| **Python GIL / threads** | Why threading does not give CPU parallelism, threading (I/O-bound) vs multiprocessing (CPU-bound) vs asyncio (single-thread concurrency) | `05` |
| **Python async / generators** | async/await + event loop, generators/yield and lazy evaluation, why they save memory | `05` |

**The bridge that plays to your strength:** you understand concurrency, memory, and scheduling deeply from Java and Go. Reason about Python and JS *from that base* out loud - "in Go you'd handle this with goroutines and a scheduler; Python's asyncio is a single-threaded cooperative version of the same idea, and the GIL is why threads don't buy you CPU parallelism." A polyglot reasoning from fundamentals reads as *more* senior than someone reciting one language's idioms. But do not oversell Python fluency - Jaimyn's deal-breaker cuts both ways.

---

## Two anchor answers to rehearse out loud (Jaimyn handed you these)

### "Explain the best you can how the useState hook works."
Skeleton to say in your own words:
- useState lets a function component hold state that survives across re-renders. You call `useState(initial)`, it returns the current value and a setter.
- React stores that state on the component's **fiber node** (its slot in the fiber tree), keyed by **call order** - which is why hooks must be called unconditionally, in the same order every render (rules of hooks).
- The value your component sees is **captured in a closure for that render**. Calling the setter does not mutate a variable, it **schedules a re-render**; on the next render, `useState` hands back the updated value.
- Setters are **batched** within an event handler (multiple sets = one re-render). Updates **replace, not merge**. If the new value derives from the old, use the **functional form** `setX(prev => ...)` to avoid stale-closure bugs.
- React uses **Object.is** to bail out if the value has not changed, and compares references - which is why you treat state as **immutable** and create new objects/arrays rather than mutating.
- Follow-ups he may push: why call-order matters (fiber slots), stale closures, batching, why not mutate, how this differs from class `this.setState`.

### "How does the JavaScript event loop work?"
Skeleton:
- JS is **single-threaded** with one **call stack**. Synchronous code runs to completion on the stack.
- Async work (timers, I/O, fetch) is handed to the **host** (browser/Node) APIs; when it completes, its callback is **queued**, not run immediately.
- The **event loop**: when the call stack is empty, it takes the next callback and pushes it on. There are two priority levels - the **microtask queue** (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`) is drained **completely after each task**, before the next macrotask or render; the **macrotask/task queue** (`setTimeout`, I/O, UI events) yields **one task per turn**.
- That ordering is why a resolved **promise callback runs before `setTimeout(0)`**. `async/await` is sugar over promises: `await` yields control back to the loop and resumes the continuation as a **microtask**.
- Consequence: long synchronous work **blocks everything** - rendering, input - so you offload with async or Web Workers.
- Follow-ups he may push: microtask vs macrotask ordering, starvation, `requestAnimationFrame` timing, Node's loop phases (timers/poll/check).

Practice both cold, no notes, out loud, until they are automatic. Then have someone fire "go deeper" on a random branch.

---

## Logistics (the joke was a real signal)
- Be **seated and connected 5 minutes early.** Never late.
- **Quiet, professional, indoors.** Neutral background, good light. Not a park, not walking.
- Dressed for a senior interview. Camera on, framed properly.
- **Test camera, mic, and connection beforehand.** A tech scramble at 3:30 costs you the opening.
- Have water, and your one-page opener notes off to the side (for you, not on camera).

---

## Detailed step-by-step revision plan
Runway: **Wed evening + all of Thursday + Friday morning.** Rebalanced for the intel: heavy on fundamentals drilling and the opening narrative; the FastMCP build is now optional, not central, because Tom drills fundamentals, not Virgin's product architecture.

### Wednesday (tonight) - Foundation + opening - ~2.5-3 hrs
1. **(45 min)** Read this doc and `01` (fit map). Internalise the two governing facts: limit-finding drill, and resume-reality is the deal-breaker.
2. **(60 min)** Build your **opening**. Write the 2-minute ANZ Plus productionisation pitch (what it did, your actual slice, guardrails, observability, evals, reliability). Under each point, write the next **two layers of drill-down** you would give. Read it aloud 3 times.
3. **(30 min)** Prep AccessBuddy as the optional second project - lighter, same productionisation lens.
4. **(15 min)** Skim `04a`, `04`, `05` headings so you know Thursday's terrain.

### Thursday - Fundamentals to depth - full day
**Morning: JavaScript + React (~3 hrs)**
1. **(75 min)** `04a` - event loop, micro/macrotask, closures, GC, promises. Write the **event-loop answer** in your own words; say it aloud until fluent. Drill: "what logs first, the promise or setTimeout(0), and why."
2. **(75 min)** `04` - useState internals, useEffect, deps, immutability, batching, stale closures. Write the **useState answer**; say it aloud.
3. **(30 min)** Answer both anchor questions **cold, no notes**, out loud. Record yourself if useful.

**Afternoon: Python (~3 hrs)**
4. **(90 min)** `05` - reference counting + generational GC, the GIL, threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio, async/await, generators. Map each to Jaimyn's list (memory / threads / async / GC). Rehearse the Go/Java-to-Python bridge lines out loud.
5. **(60 min)** *Optional* - stand up a tiny FastAPI async endpoint with a Pydantic model, only if fundamentals above are already solid. It reinforces async fluency and makes "I have been building with FastAPI recently" true. Skip without guilt if you are not fluent on the fundamentals yet - those come first.
6. **(30 min)** Skim `02`/`02a` to refresh productionisation vocab (guardrails, evals, observability) so drill-downs into your ANZ opener have depth on tap.

**Evening: full mock (~1 hr)**
7. Do the **opening pitch cold**, then have someone (or self-simulate) fire the two anchor questions plus three "why / go deeper" probes. **Rehearse the limit-admission move explicitly:** "I would reason about it like X; the edge of what I am certain on is Y; here is how I would confirm." Practising this is as important as the content - it is the behaviour Tom is grading.

### Friday morning - light polish - until ~1pm
1. **(30 min)** Re-read your opening pitch + drill ladder. One aloud run.
2. **(30 min)** Re-say the two anchor answers. Skim the one-line summaries for GC, event loop, GIL.
3. **(20 min)** Review questions to ask Tom (`01`, tuned technical - eval/LLMOps maturity, how the AI team draws boundaries with Data Science/Platform).
4. **(logistics)** Test camera/mic/connection. Quiet professional room. Dressed. Seated 5 min early.
5. **No new material after ~1pm.** Eat, rest, walk. Arrive fresh, not crammed.

---

## The one sentence to carry in
Open with the project you can be drilled on forever because it is true and it is yours; reason out loud from fundamentals; and when you reach your limit, name it cleanly and reason past it - because Tom is measuring how you think at the edge, not whether you have memorised everything.

1. **(75 min)** `04a` - event loop, micro/macrotask, closures, GC, promises. Write the **event-loop answer** in your own words; say it aloud until fluent. Drill: "what logs first, the promise or setTimeout(0), and why."

5. **(60 min)** *Optional* - stand up a tiny FastAPI async endpoint with a Pydantic model, only if fundamentals above are already solid. It reinforces async fluency and makes "I have been building with FastAPI recently" true. Skip without guilt if you are not fluent on the fundamentals yet - those come first.
6. **(30 min)** Skim `02`/`02a` to refresh productionisation vocab (guardrails, evals, observability) so drill-downs into your ANZ opener have depth on tap.

**Evening: full mock (~1 hr)**
7. Do the **opening pitch cold**, then have someone (or self-simulate) fire the two anchor questions plus three "why / go deeper" probes. **Rehearse the limit-admission move explicitly:** "I would reason about it like X; the edge of what I am certain on is Y; here is how I would confirm." Practising this is as important as the content - it is the behaviour Tom is grading.

### Friday morning - light polish - until ~1pm
1. **(30 min)** Re-read your opening pitch + drill ladder. One aloud run.
2. **(30 min)** Re-say the two anchor answers. Skim the one-line summaries for GC, event loop, GIL.
3. **(20 min)** Review questions to ask Tom (`01`, tuned technical - eval/LLMOps maturity, how the AI team draws boundaries with Data Science/Platform).
4. **(logistics)** Test camera/mic/connection. Quiet professional room. Dressed. Seated 5 min early.
5. **No new material after ~1pm.** Eat, rest, walk. Arrive fresh, not crammed.

---

## The one sentence to carry in
Open with the project you can be drilled on forever because it is true and it is yours; reason out loud from fundamentals; and when you reach your limit, name it cleanly and reason past it - because Tom is measuring how you think at the edge, not whether you have memorised everything.

# Virgin Australia - Senior AI Engineer - Interview Prep Pack

Prep for the Virgin Australia Senior AI Engineer role (Brisbane, CIO/AI team, reports to Head of AI). Round 1 is run by Harry (engineer) and the engineering lead; round 2, if reached, is the Head of AI and possibly Jaimyn.

## What the round actually is (from Jaimyn)
- High-level and conversational. No coding challenge, no leetcode.
- A few very specific pointed questions to test depth across AI systems, frontend JavaScript/React, and Python/APIs, plus some higher-level problem-solving.
- They do not expect you to get everything right or go into too much detail. Confident articulation in your own words beats exhaustive recall.
- Using AI at all during the interview is an instant fail. So this pack is for genuine learning. Read it out loud, do not memorise, be able to explain each idea as yourself.

## The pack
| File | Covers | Who |
|---|---|---|
| `01-pd-decode-and-fit.md` | The PD decoded, fit map (strong / bridge / honest gaps), your narrative spine, questions to ask them | strategic |
| `02-ai-systems-fundamentals.md` | RAG, embeddings/vector DBs, agents & tool calling, safety/guardrails, evals, LLMOps - all tied to your ANZ work | core (Jaimyn's list) |
| `02a-ai-safety-systems.md` | Dedicated safety treatment: threat surface, three-layer guardrails, prompt injection, red-teaming, safety evals, responsible AI | core (Jaimyn's list) |
| `03-fastapi-and-fastmcp.md` | FastAPI fundamentals + MCP/FastMCP, every concept bridged from your Spring/Go background | core (PD stack) |
| `04-react-hooks.md` | useState/useEffect/useMemo/useCallback, rules of hooks, RSC, modern data fetching | core (Jaimyn's list) |
| `04a-javascript-and-typescript.md` | JavaScript language fundamentals (event loop, closures, this, prototypes) + TypeScript (structural typing, generics) | core (Jaimyn's list) |
| `05-senior-python.md` | GIL, generators, async, decorators, typing, dataclasses/Pydantic, testing - via Go/Java analogies | core (PD stack) |
| `06-chatgpt-apps-and-virgin-build.md` | How a ChatGPT App works, how Virgin's flight search is built, how you would build and operate one | differentiator |
| `07-limsoc-ai-design-examples.md` | Seven LIMSOC AI initiatives, high-level staff-level designs + the platform framing + build sequencing | applied-AI portfolio |

## How the workstreams you asked for map to the pack
1. Brush up on the PD/job ad -> `01` (full decode and fit map).
2. FastAPI fundamentals -> `03` (plus FastMCP, which the PD lists and which is what Virgin's ChatGPT app is built on).
3. Senior-level Python -> `05`.
4. Jaimyn's key things (RAG/safety/evals + frontend JavaScript/React + Python/API) -> `02`, `02a` (safety), `04`, `04a` (JS/TS), `03`, `05`.
5. LIMSOC enhancements as a staff-level AI engineer -> `07` (seven initiatives designed: brief auto-summarisation, entity extraction, data-entry correction, SOP coaching, completeness assurance, ETA prediction, post-incident review).
6. (Your additions) Building a ChatGPT app + how Virgin's flight search works -> `06`.

## Suggested study order
1. `01` first - it frames everything and tells you where to lean and where to be honest.
2. `02` - the heart of the AI questions, and your strongest ground because of ANZ.
3. `06` - the differentiator; ties FastMCP, agents, evals, and Virgin's own product together.
4. `03` and `05` - the stack fundamentals, read the "if they ask" answers aloud.
5. `04` - React hooks, lighter touch, you are competent here already.
6. `07` - your applied-AI portfolio; lead with the platform framing, go deep on initiative 4 (SOP coaching/RAG) or 6 (ETA, where you show you know when not to use an LLM).

## The two things to nail above all else
1. **Convert knowledge questions into credibility moments.** Answer the concept in two sentences, then ground it in something you actually built. "The way this showed up for me was at ANZ Plus..." Your real RAG/guardrails/observability/evals experience is your edge over candidates who only know the theory.
2. **The Virgin ChatGPT app thread (`06`).** Their flagship AI product is a ChatGPT App, which is an MCP server, which is why FastMCP is in the PD. If you can reason about how it is built and operated, you are demonstrating their product and their stack at once. This is your single best card.

## Standing reminders (your positioning rules)
- Recommendation first, then reasoning. No sycophancy. Australian English, no em dashes, direct.
- ANZ and Macquarie lead. AccessBuddy is a supplementary engineering example, never the headline.
- Saying "I have not used X" cleanly, then bridging to the transferable concept, reads as senior. Bluffing reads as junior and the pointed questions will expose it.
- Do not volunteer GPA. Do not use "this is exactly the work I already do" constructions.

# PD Decode and Fit Map - Virgin Senior AI Engineer

How to use this doc: this turns the position description into a fit map so you know, before you walk in, where you are obviously strong, where you bridge from adjacent experience, and where the honest gaps are and how to handle them. Round 1 is run by Harry (engineer who started when Jaimyn did) and the engineering lead. Round 2, if you get there, is the Head of AI and possibly Jaimyn.

---

## The role in one line
Senior AI Engineer, CIO Division / AI team, Brisbane, reports to Head of AI, Level 2B, no direct reports. A hands-on applied-AI plus full-stack engineer who ships production AI systems and is trusted with the delivery realities: testing, evaluation, observability, safe rollout, and stakeholder communication. This is an individual-contributor senior role with mentoring expectations, not a management role.

## What Virgin actually wants (read between the lines)
The PD says it three times in different words: "recognising the realities of delivery, trade-offs and compromise", "what it takes to deliver production-ready solutions, including testing, evaluation and observability", "technical excellence while recognising the realities of delivery". They have been burned by, or are guarding against, people who can prototype with an LLM but cannot operate it in production. Your entire career is production engineering rigour in regulated, high-stakes environments. That is the centre of your fit. Lead with it.

---

## Fit map: requirement → your evidence → confidence

### Strong (claim directly, with receipts)
| PD requirement | Your evidence |
|---|---|
| 3+ years production-grade systems | 6.5 years, senior/lead, ANZ + Macquarie + Leidos |
| Hands-on with LLMs (RAG, tool/function calling) | ANZ Plus generative-AI search platform on Vertex AI/Gemini, you owned the search/retrieval APIs |
| Cross-functional delivery (Product, Eng, Security, Legal/Privacy, Ops) | Regulated banking at ANZ; defined requirements directly with business at Macquarie; seven-jurisdiction stakeholder alignment at SLSA |
| Safety/guardrails, responsible AI | Established generative-AI guardrails in a risk-averse banking context |
| Observability (metrics, logs, traces) | OpenTelemetry across ANZ, Macquarie, AccessBuddy; Sentry, Better Stack |
| Security & privacy (IAM, secrets, PII, auditability) | Regulated banking; Secure Code Warrior; AWS Solutions Architect; data discovery for a critical govt agency at Leidos |
| Software engineering best practice (testing, CI/CD, design reviews) | TDD with 80%+ coverage enforced at ANZ and Macquarie; GitHub Actions, Bitbucket Pipelines |
| Agile delivery, roadmap ownership, estimation, stakeholder comms | Scrum Master scaling 2→6 teams in SAFe; LIMSOC product ownership and roadmap; exec presentations |
| Communicate to non-technical / executive audiences | Authored and presented national strategy to executive leadership; C-suite presentations |
| AWS cloud concepts | AWS Solutions Architect Associate; AWS used at ANZ, Macquarie, Leidos |
| Mentoring junior engineers | Mentored juniors at Macquarie; coached teams as Scrum Master |
| React + TypeScript | Macquarie real-time portal, Leidos rewrite, AccessBuddy Next.js |

### Bridge (true, but you adapt from adjacent ground, say so confidently)
| PD requirement | How you bridge |
|---|---|
| Python as primary language | You have used Python (Macquarie, ANZ stack) but Go and Java are your deepest. Bridge: strong polyglot, fluent in Python, and you reason about it from a deep systems base. See the senior-Python doc. Do not oversell, do not apologise. |
| FastAPI / FastMCP | Not used in production. Bridge: you know API design deeply (gRPC/Protobuf/REST, Google AIP standards at ANZ), FastAPI is a clean Python framing of the same concerns, and MCP is the protocol behind Virgin's own ChatGPT app. You have clearly done the reading. See the FastAPI/FastMCP doc and the ChatGPT Apps doc. |
| Advanced RAG | You built the retrieval side of a real RAG platform. Bridge: you have lived the core (retrieval quality, grounding, guardrails); the "advanced" techniques (re-ranking, hybrid, agentic RAG) you can discuss fluently. See the AI fundamentals doc. |
| Agentic systems (planning, memory) | You drove AI integration strategy and guardrails; agents are the next step. Bridge: you understand the loop, the risks, and the constraint-first design philosophy. |
| AWS (vs your GCP depth) | Your hands-on cloud depth is GCP (Cloud Run, Spanner, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, BigQuery). Bridge: AWS Solutions Architect certified, AWS used across roles, and cloud concepts transfer; you map GCP service to AWS equivalent comfortably (Cloud Run≈ECS/Fargate/App Runner, Pub/Sub≈SNS/SQS/EventBridge, BigQuery≈Redshift/Athena, Spanner≈Aurora/DynamoDB). |

### Honest gaps (do not hide, handle cleanly)
| Gap | Handling |
|---|---|
| Databricks (MLflow / Mosaic AI) | You have not used it. It is a desirable, not essential. Honest line: "I have not worked in Databricks specifically, I have worked across the GCP data stack, BigQuery, Dataflow, Spanner. I understand the lakehouse pattern and MLflow's role as a model registry and experiment tracker, and picking up a managed platform is not where I see risk." Then pivot to the transferable concept (registries, experiment tracking, automated evals) which you do understand. |
| pgvector / AWS Cognitive Search specifically | Concept is solid (you run Postgres, you understand vector search and ANN). You have not used pgvector in anger. Say the concept clearly and be honest you have not shipped on it. |
| Airline/travel domain | Desirable, not essential. You have zero airline experience and should not pretend otherwise. Counter-weight: you have deep regulated, safety-critical, real-time operational domain experience (banking, plus literal coastal emergency operations through LIMSOC). The mental model of safety-critical, real-time, high-consequence systems transfers; the domain specifics you would learn fast. |
| LangGraph / LangChain | Desirable. Know what they are (LangChain = LLM app framework/abstractions; LangGraph = graph/state-machine for controllable agent flows). Honest: you have read on them and understand the orchestration problem they solve, you have not built production on them. |

---

## The narrative spine for this interview (your layered story)
This is the exact thing the BCG post-mortem flagged: have a 90-second headline and pre-built 2-3 minute expansions per beat so "expand on the second pass" is mechanical.

**Headline (90 sec):** "I am a senior engineer who has spent the last few years on production AI in regulated environments. At ANZ Plus I owned the search APIs inside a generative-AI search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini, drove the AI integration strategy for the team, and put guardrails around generative AI in a context where a wrong answer has compliance consequences. Before that I architected a real-time asset platform at Macquarie. Alongside that I have built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, so I have full-stack and operational ownership end to end. What I care about is the gap between an AI demo and a production AI system, retrieval quality, evaluation, guardrails, observability, and I bring the testing and operational discipline that closes it."

**Expansion beats (each 2-3 min, have a concrete scene ready):**
1. The ANZ RAG/search platform: what it did, your piece, the model-selection and scaling decisions, the guardrails.
2. Guardrails in a regulated context: a specific control you put in and why.
3. Macquarie real-time platform: architecture decision, the event-driven design, the 50-hours-a-week saved.
4. AccessBuddy: full-stack solo ownership, the operational side (observability, CI/CD), why it proves breadth not just a side project.
5. Stakeholder/exec communication: the LIMSOC national strategy presented to executive leadership, seven-jurisdiction alignment.

---

## Questions to ask them (signals seniority and genuine interest)
- "Where is the AI team on the build-vs-buy line, how much is building on foundation models and orchestration versus training/fine-tuning your own?"
- "The flight-search app in ChatGPT is live, what is the architecture behind it, and what is the roadmap, partner airlines and international were mentioned publicly?" (shows you did the homework, ties to MCP)
- "How mature is the eval and LLMOps tooling today, and where do you most want to lift it?" (signals you think about the production realities they emphasised)
- "How is the AI team set up relative to Data Science and Platform Engineering, where are the boundaries?"
- "What does the first six months look like for someone in this role, what would success be?"
- For the Head of AI in round 2: "What is your thesis on where AI gives Virgin the most leverage, customer experience, operations, or revenue/loyalty?" (the PD names all three)

---

## Tone reminders (from your standing positioning rules)
- Recommendation first, then reasoning. No sycophancy.
- Australian English, no em dashes, direct.
- AccessBuddy is supplementary proof, a personal full-stack build that proves breadth and operational ownership, never the headline. For this engineering AI role it is allowed as a genuine engineering example, but ANZ and Macquarie lead.
- Do not volunteer GPA. Address only if asked.
- Do not use "this is exactly the work I already do" constructions. State the capability directly.
- It is fine and good to say "I have not used X" cleanly and pivot to the transferable concept. Honesty plus a strong bridge reads as senior. Bluffing reads as junior, and Jaimyn warned the questions are pointed enough to expose a bluff.

# PD Decode and Fit Map - Virgin Senior AI Engineer

How to use this doc: this turns the position description into a fit map so you know, before you walk in, where you are obviously strong, where you bridge from adjacent experience, and where the honest gaps are and how to handle them. Round 1 is run by Harry (engineer who started when Jaimyn did) and the engineering lead. **Round 2 is with Tom, the Head of AI - a deeply technical limit-finding drill; see `09-round-2-tom-deep-technical.md` for the definitive round-2 prep and plan.**

---

## The role in one line
Senior AI Engineer, CIO Division / AI team, Brisbane, reports to Head of AI, Level 2B, no direct reports. A hands-on applied-AI plus full-stack engineer who ships production AI systems and is trusted with the delivery realities: testing, evaluation, observability, safe rollout, and stakeholder communication. This is an individual-contributor senior role with mentoring expectations, not a management role.

## What Virgin actually wants (read between the lines)
The PD says it three times in different words: "recognising the realities of delivery, trade-offs and compromise", "what it takes to deliver production-ready solutions, including testing, evaluation and observability", "technical excellence while recognising the realities of delivery". They have been burned by, or are guarding against, people who can prototype with an LLM but cannot operate it in production. Your entire career is production engineering rigour in regulated, high-stakes environments. That is the centre of your fit. Lead with it.

---

## Fit map: requirement → your evidence → confidence

### Strong (claim directly, with receipts)
| PD requirement | Your evidence |
|---|---|
| 3+ years production-grade systems | 6.5 years, senior/lead, ANZ + Macquarie + Leidos |
| Hands-on with LLMs (RAG, tool/function calling) | ANZ Plus generative-AI search platform on Vertex AI/Gemini, you owned the search/retrieval APIs |
| Cross-functional delivery (Product, Eng, Security, Legal/Privacy, Ops) | Regulated banking at ANZ; defined requirements directly with business at Macquarie; seven-jurisdiction stakeholder alignment at SLSA |
| Safety/guardrails, responsible AI | Established generative-AI guardrails in a risk-averse banking context |
| Observability (metrics, logs, traces) | OpenTelemetry across ANZ, Macquarie, AccessBuddy; Sentry, Better Stack |
| Security & privacy (IAM, secrets, PII, auditability) | Regulated banking; Secure Code Warrior; AWS Solutions Architect; data discovery for a critical govt agency at Leidos |
| Software engineering best practice (testing, CI/CD, design reviews) | TDD with 80%+ coverage enforced at ANZ and Macquarie; GitHub Actions, Bitbucket Pipelines |
| Agile delivery, roadmap ownership, estimation, stakeholder comms | Scrum Master scaling 2→6 teams in SAFe; LIMSOC product ownership and roadmap; exec presentations |
| Communicate to non-technical / executive audiences | Authored and presented national strategy to executive leadership; C-suite presentations |
| AWS cloud concepts | AWS Solutions Architect Associate; AWS used at ANZ, Macquarie, Leidos |
| Mentoring junior engineers | Mentored juniors at Macquarie; coached teams as Scrum Master |
| React + TypeScript | Macquarie real-time portal, Leidos rewrite, AccessBuddy Next.js |

### Bridge (true, but you adapt from adjacent ground, say so confidently)
| PD requirement | How you bridge |
|---|---|
| Python as primary language | You have used Python (Macquarie, ANZ stack) but Go and Java are your deepest. Bridge: strong polyglot, fluent in Python, and you reason about it from a deep systems base. See the senior-Python doc. Do not oversell, do not apologise. |
| FastAPI / FastMCP | Not used in production. Bridge: you know API design deeply (gRPC/Protobuf/REST, Google AIP standards at ANZ), FastAPI is a clean Python framing of the same concerns, and MCP is the protocol behind Virgin's own ChatGPT app. You have clearly done the reading. See the FastAPI/FastMCP doc and the ChatGPT Apps doc. |
| Advanced RAG | You built the retrieval side of a real RAG platform. Bridge: you have lived the core (retrieval quality, grounding, guardrails); the "advanced" techniques (re-ranking, hybrid, agentic RAG) you can discuss fluently. See the AI fundamentals doc. |
| Agentic systems (planning, memory) | You drove AI integration strategy and guardrails; agents are the next step. Bridge: you understand the loop, the risks, and the constraint-first design philosophy. |
| AWS (vs your GCP depth) | Your hands-on cloud depth is GCP (Cloud Run, Spanner, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, BigQuery). Bridge: AWS Solutions Architect certified, AWS used across roles, and cloud concepts transfer; you map GCP service to AWS equivalent comfortably (Cloud Run≈ECS/Fargate/App Runner, Pub/Sub≈SNS/SQS/EventBridge, BigQuery≈Redshift/Athena, Spanner≈Aurora/DynamoDB). |

### Honest gaps (do not hide, handle cleanly)
| Gap | Handling |
|---|---|
| Databricks (MLflow / Mosaic AI) | You have not used it. It is a desirable, not essential. Honest line: "I have not worked in Databricks specifically, I have worked across the GCP data stack, BigQuery, Dataflow, Spanner. I understand the lakehouse pattern and MLflow's role as a model registry and experiment tracker, and picking up a managed platform is not where I see risk." Then pivot to the transferable concept (registries, experiment tracking, automated evals) which you do understand. |
| pgvector / AWS Cognitive Search specifically | Concept is solid (you run Postgres, you understand vector search and ANN). You have not used pgvector in anger. Say the concept clearly and be honest you have not shipped on it. |
| Airline/travel domain | Desirable, not essential. You have zero airline experience and should not pretend otherwise. Counter-weight: you have deep regulated, safety-critical, real-time operational domain experience (banking, plus literal coastal emergency operations through LIMSOC). The mental model of safety-critical, real-time, high-consequence systems transfers; the domain specifics you would learn fast. |
| LangGraph / LangChain | Desirable. Know what they are (LangChain = LLM app framework/abstractions; LangGraph = graph/state-machine for controllable agent flows). Honest: you have read on them and understand the orchestration problem they solve, you have not built production on them. |

---

## The narrative spine for this interview (your layered story)
This is the exact thing the BCG post-mortem flagged: have a 90-second headline and pre-built 2-3 minute expansions per beat so "expand on the second pass" is mechanical.

**Headline (90 sec):** "I am a senior engineer who has spent the last few years on production AI in regulated environments. At ANZ Plus I owned the search APIs inside a generative-AI search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini, drove the AI integration strategy for the team, and put guardrails around generative AI in a context where a wrong answer has compliance consequences. Before that I architected a real-time asset platform at Macquarie. Alongside that I have built and shipped a multi-tenant SaaS solo, so I have full-stack and operational ownership end to end. What I care about is the gap between an AI demo and a production AI system, retrieval quality, evaluation, guardrails, observability, and I bring the testing and operational discipline that closes it."

**Expansion beats (each 2-3 min, have a concrete scene ready):**
1. The ANZ RAG/search platform: what it did, your piece, the model-selection and scaling decisions, the guardrails.
2. Guardrails in a regulated context: a specific control you put in and why.
3. Macquarie real-time platform: architecture decision, the event-driven design, the 50-hours-a-week saved.
4. AccessBuddy: full-stack solo ownership, the operational side (observability, CI/CD), why it proves breadth not just a side project.
5. Stakeholder/exec communication: the LIMSOC national strategy presented to executive leadership, seven-jurisdiction alignment.

---

## Questions to ask them (signals seniority and genuine interest)
- "Where is the AI team on the build-vs-buy line, how much is building on foundation models and orchestration versus training/fine-tuning your own?"
- "The flight-search app in ChatGPT is live, what is the architecture behind it, and what is the roadmap, partner airlines and international were mentioned publicly?" (shows you did the homework, ties to MCP)
- "How mature is the eval and LLMOps tooling today, and where do you most want to lift it?" (signals you think about the production realities they emphasised)
- "How is the AI team set up relative to Data Science and Platform Engineering, where are the boundaries?"
- "What does the first six months look like for someone in this role, what would success be?"
- For the Head of AI in round 2: "What is your thesis on where AI gives Virgin the most leverage, customer experience, operations, or revenue/loyalty?" (the PD names all three)

---

## Tone reminders (from your standing positioning rules)
- Recommendation first, then reasoning. No sycophancy.
- Australian English, no em dashes, direct.
- AccessBuddy is supplementary proof, a personal full-stack build that proves breadth and operational ownership, never the headline. For this engineering AI role it is allowed as a genuine engineering example, but ANZ and Macquarie lead.
- Do not volunteer GPA. Address only if asked.
- Do not use "this is exactly the work I already do" constructions. State the capability directly.
- It is fine and good to say "I have not used X" cleanly and pivot to the transferable concept. Honesty plus a strong bridge reads as senior. Bluffing reads as junior, and Jaimyn warned the questions are pointed enough to expose a bluff.
